831.quote_or_event: “The nights are wasted sleeping, and the days are wasted eating. Human life is such a precious jewel, but it is being lost in exchange for a mere shell. … You fool - you shall regret and repent in the end!”
831.explanation: Guru Nanak calls it folly to trade the jewel of human life for a worthless shell, and warns that the fool will regret it.
831.tie_back: The Kural defines folly as grabbing what harms you and letting gain slip away; Guru Nanak's fool who swaps a jewel for a shell makes exactly this losing trade.
831.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 156, Raag Gauri Bairagan, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
831._accuracy_note: Strong on folly as a losing exchange; in Gurbani the gain thrown away is the human life given for remembering God, a spiritual rather than practical ledger.

832.quote_or_event: “Like the monkey with a handful of grain, who will not let go because of greed - just so, all the deeds committed in greed ultimately become a noose around one’s neck.”
832.explanation: Kabir uses the monkey trapped because it will not let go of a fistful of grain to show how deeds done from greed tighten into a noose.
832.tie_back: The Kural calls it the worst folly to set one's heart on unfitting deeds; Kabir's monkey clinging to what traps it shows that attachment.
832.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 336, Raag Gauri, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
832._accuracy_note: Partial: Kabir targets greed (lobh) as a trap, while the Kural speaks more broadly of loving deeds unfit for one's conduct or ability.

833.quote_or_event: “Those who are totally blind in their minds, do not have the integrity to keep their word. … Some do not know the Sound-current of the Naad, spiritual wisdom or the joy of song. They do not even understand good and bad.”
833.explanation: Guru Nanak lists the marks of the inwardly blind: no integrity in keeping their word, no taste for wisdom or song, and no grasp of good and bad.
833.tie_back: The Kural catalogues the habits of the fool, shamelessness, not seeking, lacking affection and cherishing nothing; Guru Nanak gives a similar list of inner lacks.
833.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1411, Saloks Vaaran Te Vadheek (salok 15), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
833._accuracy_note: Next-best: both are lists of a fool's lacks, but the items differ; Gurbani does not name shamelessness or lack of affection here.

834.quote_or_event: “He says one thing, and does something else. There is no love in his heart, and yet with his mouth he talks tall. … One who does not practice what he preaches to others, shall come and go in reincarnation, through birth and death.”
834.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib Guru Arjan condemns the person who teaches others but does not live by it, and says such a one stays bound to birth and death.
834.tie_back: The Kural calls the person who studies, understands and teaches others but does not live by it the greatest fool; Guru Arjan names the same failure and its cost.
834.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 269, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib (ashtapadi 5, stanza 7), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
834._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on preaching without practising; Gurbani adds the result of further rebirth where the Kural simply calls it the height of folly.

835.quote_or_event: “Vibrate, and meditate on the Lord of the Universe, and never forget Him. This is the blessed opportunity of this human incarnation. … Otherwise, you shall regret and repent afterwards, and you shall not be carried across to the other side.”
835.explanation: Kabir teaches that this one human birth is the chance to be freed from the round of births; wasted, it leads to regret and to staying in that round.
835.tie_back: The Kural says the fool can make in one life the suffering of seven births; Kabir likewise says the chance of this single life, once wasted, keeps one bound to rebirth.
835.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1159, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
835._accuracy_note: Strong on one life deciding many to come; Gurbani speaks of reincarnation and not being carried across, not the Kural's hell (alaru).

836.quote_or_event: “If a fool does a job, he cannot do it right. Even if he does something right, he does the next thing wrong.”
836.explanation: In Asa Ki Vaar Guru Angad observes that whatever task a fool takes up goes wrong, and even a success is followed by a fresh mistake.
836.tie_back: The Kural says that when a fool who does not know the way takes up a task, the work fails; Guru Angad says the same of the fool's undertakings.
836.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa, Asa Ki Vaar (salok 5 before pauri 22), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
836._accuracy_note: Close on the fool's work failing; the Kural's second penalty, that he puts himself in chains, is not in this salok.

837.quote_or_event: “Your wealth shall not go with you; why do you cling to it, you fool? Children, friends, family and spouse - who of these shall accompany you? … The fool does not acknowledge the One who gave this; forgetting the Naam, O Nanak! He will repent in the end.”
837.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib Guru Arjan asks the fool why he clings to wealth that will not stay with him and forgets the One who gave it.
837.tie_back: The Kural says that when a fool gains great wealth, strangers enjoy it while his own go hungry; Guru Arjan also shows the fool's wealth slipping away from him and his family.
837.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 288, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib (ashtapadi 19, stanza 5), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
837._accuracy_note: Next-best only: both speak of the fool and his wealth, but Gurbani's point is its impermanence and forgetting the Giver, not strangers feasting while kin starve.

838.quote_or_event: “One person brings a full bottle, and another fills his cup. Drinking the wine, his intelligence departs, and madness enters his mind; he cannot distinguish between his own and others, and he is struck down by his Lord and Master.”
838.explanation: Guru Amar Das describes how wine drives out intelligence and brings in madness, so a man can no longer tell his own from others; Sikh teaching rejects intoxicants.
838.tie_back: The Kural likens a fool who gains something to a madman who is also drunk; Guru Amar Das's picture of drink bringing madness gives the same image of reason lost.
838.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 554, Raag Bihaagraa, Bihaagre Ki Vaar (salok 1 before pauri 16), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
838._accuracy_note: Matches the drink-and-madness image well; Gurbani is warning against actual intoxication, while the Kural uses it as a simile for a fool with wealth or power.

839.quote_or_event: “Friendship with a fool never works out right. As he knows, he acts; behold, and see that it is so. … Friendship with a fool, and love with a pompous person, are like lines drawn in water, leaving no trace or mark.”
839.explanation: In two saloks of Asa Ki Vaar Guru Angad says friendship with a fool never works out, and that it is like a line drawn in water, gone without a trace.
839.tie_back: The Kural's ironic praise is that friendship with fools is sweet because parting from it leaves no pain; Guru Angad's line drawn in water leaves the same lack of any mark.
839.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa, Asa Ki Vaar (saloks 3 and 4 before pauri 22), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
839._accuracy_note: Very close in theme and image; the Kural is ironic about painless parting, while Guru Angad stresses the bond's lack of substance.

840.quote_or_event: “Seeing the swans swimming, the herons became envious. But the poor herons drowned and died, and floated with their heads down, and their feet above.”
840.explanation: Guru Amar Das tells of herons who envied the swans and tried to swim among them, only to drown in disgrace.
840.tie_back: The Kural says a fool entering the assembly of the wise is like unwashed feet on a clean bed; Guru Amar Das's herons venturing among the swans are likewise out of place.
840.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 585, Raag Vadahans, Vadahans Ki Vaar (salok 3 before pauri 1), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
840._accuracy_note: Good on the unworthy intruding among the noble; the Kural stresses the defilement of the gathering, Gurbani the disgrace that befalls the intruder.
